text: The Ache to Express: A Meditation on Art I. Art, To Me Art is the expression of one, the understandable, or the opposite of it—the unfathomable—to others. The discovery of the ‘self,’ if it so exists, is the portion of

art, to which it is indebted and before which its authority submits. Art is what one yearns for when the poison of life seems inevitable to be wedded with. Just like Socrates drank the hemlock, which remains a memorable moment

in history—can be expressed, in the field of art. For one to be alive, for one to exhibit their own-self, or to hold true something which a large contingent or the populace generally considers it absurd or peculiar, is art.

Have a moment of art with thyself, and gaze into the depths of thy soul, for you shall find the fire of expression, be it moral or immoral, in yourself. When the poet expresses himself to his beloved, or the

artist speaks volumes in the painting buried in the soul of himself, or when the orator speaks of what the ordinary implants in his head, but a little, that is the experience of art in the strings of this existence.

What is art, to me? My expression shall be paradoxical, I am aware, but metaphorically, I shall make it my duty to make it clear; art, to me, is when one dances with the idols, or has intercourse with the

shape of oneself, or to be intimate with the being of the existence with the peculiarity—the atypical nature of being—to possess the birthing power of expression, to lay bare what one demands of existence in the enigmatic strings of time.

If I may be allowed to dive deeper into this; to the one who lives, not survives, is the artist. Let there be no misunderstanding of the weight of the metaphors I have profusely offered, but to plant the seed
of a notion of truth, I must delve into the ground of it, and then raise the bars, if I may be able to, and soar high in the clouds. In essence: the expression of one to all, intimately, consciously,

and profoundly is, to me, to be art. 2. Living And Use Of Art Every human—walking, living, breathing—holds within themselves the capacity to exhibit the self, not just for inner strength but to explore and shape the world. This exhibiting

impulse, as we derived earlier, is art. Any human who meets this criterion, broad though it may be, holds the power to express. Whether to others or inwardly, this expression affirms life. It is always for this; that man has
fought and dried himself. For if he were to allow the fire of his own-self be watered, wet, that would be the case for him to breathe not, nor for him to live, but his survival is not the issue

here. It is for this inexorable thirst that man fought, lived, claimed his creations as his own—he bought them, bore them, became them. His inability to let go—that is art. Art is the vastness of eternity, and the extensibility of

it is ever growing. It is not merely music, song, poetry, painting—nay—such shallowness does not capture its depth. Anyhow, I would like you, my dear reader, to think here with me: did wars not happen for land because it was

associated with a certain specific people? Or was it not that Van Gogh explains himself, or perhaps his perception in his paintings? Or is it not that the language of the Pukhtoons is so dear to them that they take

it not for paltry price? I ask you once more, is it not that the inability to divorce Shakespeare by the Britishers is a sign of art? We live for language, poetry, music, paintings, oration, looks, and the like—this is

art—which, again, is not its narrow ending tunneled exist. The ability for a human to live, live in the problem, the vastness, the ever-expansion of life, is provided to man by art. When man is struck by calamity, he goes

and finds peace in the art of his existence, or perhaps, in another humans art. The suffering of this life is grand, much more than we can fathom, and if the suffering of the dying children, or them losing their

parents, if all that is summed into a great summation, without a doubt, it is a great pain. To accompany this tragic life of ours, this tradition of sorrow—unwanted, inexorable, and deeply painful—has always been with us—and art has our

backs. In my experience of life so far, I have always turned to art, knowingly or unknowingly, be it in the form of interactions with others, or sitting in the vastness of this world, alone, with myself. Whether it was

the Greeks, the Romans, the Italians, the French, the Indians, the Persians, the Ottomans, the Chinese, all of them had an expression. And let me ask you this, ladies and gentlemen, do they still not have it? Perhaps, altered, but

is it not the same artistic style, to which they attach the bonds of their ancestors and ultimately, themselves? What is it they these great nations live for? What do they have other than their cultures, religions, their language—for which

they fight—or their dress code, ladies and gentlemen, I ask you, is it not art? 3. Art In Culture Culture is the collective representation of a population within a given region, shaped by the circumstances they inhabit or reflect upon—whether

through sense, reason, or the inherited memory of their history. It is the shape that a people carve into the chaos around them, using whatever tools they possess: myth, memory, music, ritual, resistance. It forms in the heat of necessity,

in the long echo of loss, in the quiet refusal to be forgotten. And art is the language of that refusal. Where culture is the body of a people, art is its pulse. Where culture stores the inheritance of a

society, art interrupts, challenges, or sanctifies it. They move together—sometimes in harmony, sometimes in tension—but never apart. The artist does not merely dwell in culture; he is exposed to it, burned by it, made restless by its limits. He is

not at peace. He observes what is praised but also what is suppressed. He listens not only to the voices of his time, but to those silenced, forgotten, or misremembered. It is from this tension—between the seen and unseen, the

spoken and the inexpressible—that true art is born. The artist may live among his people, but his vision often stares beyond them. He is concerned with posterity, not praise. His aim is not to flatter a people but to remind

them—sometimes cruelly, sometimes tenderly—of the truths they try to avoid. This is why, in any genuine culture, the artist is both loved and feared. The significance of art lies in its ability to create values, not just reflect them. It

does not merely decorate life; it constructs the framework upon which life is lived. Generations adopt mannerisms, moral instincts, and emotional vocabularies that were first born in poems, in songs, in paintings, in architecture, in the tragic silence of a

play. The future walks upon the ground paved by the artist’s vision. And this vision is not always beautiful in the shallow sense—it may be brutal, broken, or disquieting. But it is real. And reality, when shaped with sincerity, becomes

sacred. Culture, in this view, is not soft—it is formative. It is the setting in which the individual is produced and through which his actions gain meaning. And every system—be it a school, a university, a village bazaar, a state

religion, or a silent room in a forgotten house—bears within it a pattern, a gesture, an echo that once belonged to art. The system is the shell; the art is the seed. Even today, in an age of mechanical information

and digital sameness, culture is not dead—it is displaced, stretched, exhausted, but still vital. Art, too, suffers in this time: simplified, commodified, often misunderstood. But it remains the final place where truth still dares to stand naked. Consider Ghani Khan

Baba. His poetry is not merely literature—it is rebellion. It is the cry of a soul too alive to obey, too wounded to forget. His verse does not ask for comfort—it asks for courage. And compare that to the cold,

tragic gravity of the Russians, whose prose carries the burden of a century’s worth of collapse and silence. Their literature does not console—it mourns, it reveals, it accuses. Art is not a mere entertainment. It is the raw breath of

a people trying to explain to themselves why they continue to exist. It is culture’s most intimate mirror—and sometimes, its most savage critic. The artist does not offer certainty, but he offers a form to what we feel and fear.

And that form—that raw shaping of truth—is what gives meaning to our systems, our ethics, and our memory. Culture without art is machinery. Art without culture is a scream in a void. Together, they are the soul and body of

civilization. 4. Art In Philosophy What can a man dream of as a thinker, if there is no imagination? This imaginative body—this inner landscape that births expression—is the very core of our artistic nature. It is the first tool we

ever used, long before language was formed, before logic drew its first straight line. Man did not begin with reason—he began with wonder. And wonder demanded expression. We etched symbols into stone, smeared pigment on cavern walls, danced in rituals

under the night sky. Why? Not for utility, not for science, not for reason—but for the sheer need to externalize what we felt. That is art. That is imagination. There was a powerful and ecstatic form of expression one ought

to consider before delving into the depths and essence of things. The imaginative body of ourselves is the artistic nature, which is and can be used as a tool in many different aspects of our lives. Art was there before

anything. Humans had to expresses and make others understand, which is our nature, always has been. Thus, we originated the cave-painting. If one may ponder on the ancestry of human kind, one must come to the adaptive conclusion that the

presence of all else came forth from the presence of art to begin with. Cave-art, which is painting—but is the expressive art—came way before anything else for the understanding and reflective construction of what one had in their imagination or

what they felt. Way before philosophy existed formally, (know that philosophy has always been with us, and always will,) art was soaring in skies and forming the imaginative body of us humans, which in title we use to this day.

Philosophical inquiries are standing on the grounds of art. To be a philosopher, one must be aware of the artistic nature of expression, be it in the form of writing, as I am doing now, or painting, or lyrics, or

any other format of expression, to convey the message to those who would buy and be interested in the submission of the purpose of their own grounding deep into themselves. In the agony of it all, the philosophers who have

formed all of their prose and poetry have never given enough credit to art. The artistic nature of it is painted deep in them, whether they were aware of it or not, or whether the modern reader is aware of

it. The underestimated punctuation on the express of art and of nature, in honesty, is the ultimate example of the threat to art. In who or what they mention in their texts, and of how great a vigor they do,

they ought to represent art and form the ultimate name of art. Whether we speak of the Greeks, the Germans, the Arabs, Persians, or anyone else, their whole entirety of natural existence is formed of the basic quality and entity

of art. Imagination is not a luxury; it is the origin. Without it, the thinker has no ground to stand on. Without it, inquiry is mute. For all our systems and syllogisms, what drives us to think in the first

place is not logic—it is the ache to express something that lives beyond words. And that ache, that raw longing, is art in its purest sense. 5. The Threat to Art Living and dying, or at least to know of

life, something, is art. And this is the great human ability to which I give such great credit that has woven his spirit in the threads of eternity and chronicle which reflects upon us now. This has accompanied and assisted

us in corners of darkness, and it shall, so far, the spirit of a human life. However, unfortunately, art is the dying spirit and the death of it is by no others than the ones that originated it in the

first place, human. We live in the great age of expansion, of artificial intelligence and of great innovations of human development and of great exercise of man’s intellect is at play, so much so, that none have witnessed it before.

But amidst all this, we are step-by-step evaluating our own demise—the death of art. This is a tragic thought, one that bites me. I call this age the “age of scientific objectivity.” Now, do I have a grudge against science,
nay, it would make me a fool, a form of a man, who has no beginning of comprehension. Science is for the utility of a human, and not that alone, but it is truly giving the helping hand to our

Earth, raising it from the problems it has brought with it, the disturbances of its own existence. Science is how we live; art is why we live. And to confuse these two, or to discredit art as a whole is

an error so great that the existence of the civilization of us humans is being played with. It is, as George Orwell postulated his great novel, 1984. Although, such gloomy, desperate and death bearing society has a possibility of not

being born. Now, how is this new age so dangerous to us? I will, as you may also have experienced, perhaps better than I, the existence of ‘artificial’ entities of art, or even of such intimate prose and arts of

a human which ought to arise from the heart and the winding of it from whatever the intellect allows. But, lo and behold, the artificially generated pieces have held us in the chains of existence and made us slaves of

it. Where words of a human mattered, came with it the fake, dissolved, impregnating such things with what never came from us—artificial intelligence. Where the requirement of the soul and artistic style mattered, and where it painted the tapestry of

our own, it lies in the falsifying soul of our creation, but the systematic threads of it, in addition to that, the painting of dried cloth and paints is the example of it. The experience of it is no more,

the thought, or even the hate towards entities is no longer. Nothing seems to catch the eyes and paint the pictures of emotions or of existence any longer, as art has been handed over to the dead. Science may not

be able to provide the essence for which we shall live. This age is the dry mountains, in which there are minerals, but art is the valley in which we come across butterflies, and we are losing it. Would it
matter if all of a sudden, we lost all this? Will it matter if all this is thrown out the window? Will it matter if all of it is discarded? The answer to that, is I suppose, yes. Humans have

become a threat to their very own creation. Forgive me, ladies and gentlemen, but the truth of life is this; that we are losing the thing we are bound to keep. To Homer, to Shakespeare, to Dostoevsky, to Ghani Khan

Baba, to Ghalib, to Russell, to Goethe—they have given humanity the ability to breathe in the atmosphere of the unthinkable. These new inventions have, altogether, without a shadow of a doubt, made life miserable instead of making it worthwhile. I

come across people, even myself, if I may be allowed, who feel the emptiness of life, as if nothing in a whole muster their imagination to be birthed with something that has the ability to even repose the genuine happiness

of the soul, and all that combined in the truth of it, is dreadful. It is this, that makes me sorrowful and doubtful of the continuation of man’s life. How is it that we shall live without the expression of

art? It is to the nature of us, humans, that we are insulting. Revolutions began with art. Ideologies were carved with its chisel. Our cultures—yours and mine—are descendants of ancient artistic spirit. The past did not speak with facts; it
spoke with rhythm and symbols. Am I mad? In the modern era—maybe. I only plant this seed in your mind: Where is art now? And what are we doing to it? The dangers to the nature of art are not

one, but in unity, many. The false generation of art, via media that has the absence of feels and which is the product of “all the same” expression is harming art. Now, creation is confused with production. A man no

longer bleeds to speak; he performs what has already been accepted. The wild tongue of madness is tamed by technique. The sacred is rendered safe. The imitator receives the same praise as the original. The crowd claps—louder than ever—and so

the artist vanishes. The discrediting of art or to not even consider it and call it mere entertainment—ah, what entertainment? —what are we even speaking of? This nonsense, to bleed us into the concept of “sheep mentality” or to drag

us into such a boat where all is but a production of the same idea, to only bring forth utility. The ability to live resides in art, and we have become its enemies, naming it mere entertainment and insanity. Disgrace.
6. What Of It? It is this that we now have come to, that the ability of it to survive and for art to define itself and for art to remain, because it will be inharmonious for us to live

without art. WHAT? Without expression? Without love and pain or sorrowful attitude remaining or living in us? To have come to this, we can not only drag this into its positive line, but also to the correct format of it,
which is not the purpose of this essay. But to know and to frame its truth and its honesty into the tapestry of time, is such to be the case. If the realization of the death of art is taking

to the mountain folds, then, perhaps, may we contemplate the essence of the human relation with art. My soul aim is not to bring anything down, on the flipside, it is to bring categories up to their feet where the

formation of actuality and truth may be, where the essence of reality may have formed and where we shall realize that the core cold, inhumane in art of living and the unsolicited outcome which I suppose no one wants is

to be framed into our lives, or of those to come. The loss of the selfproclaimed expression to the modern day alltoothesame world, and the busy attitude of what has occurred in the life of a certain specific individual to
have to hold them as the pinnacle of life is the false grounding and then erection of our lives. The all too many people who hold the strings of art and manipulate it for us to be held in their

hands and for us to forget the artistic nature of the past of those who did erect it in the sense which it should be used, but the reformation is so strangely bound and so vastly improper that the blending

of us, and bleeding into all toothesame nature is desperately uncalled for. The experimental quality, or, the exploration spirit in us has, not yet, but is littlebylittle drowning into the space of unavailability of being conveyed. The core of this;

to let it come back to us. To let Van Gogh paint himself again. To let Michelangelo Di Lodovico craft his imagination for our eyes to witness. To let Friedrich Nietzsche write his poetry and prose once more. To let

Khushal Khan Khattak compose poems on Aimal Khan and Darya Afridi. To let eternity remember the echos of the French Revolution by the art of political philosophy. To let France not be destroyed by Hitler because of its beautiful art

once more. To let Homer’s mysticism bring back Odysseus back home. We are bound by, now, the chains of similarity. Which in itself is not the issue so great, but we have, because of it, lost the part of us

which has the yearning for experiments. Art is for the alive. To live, survival is necessary, but for survival, living is not necessary. A Thought on Religion I. Religion, To Me I grew up in a religious country, where religion

is worshiped and the entirety of the population considers it to be the ultimate resonating reflection of life. The irony of it seems to me to be not only its irony, but the stupidity of the situation and of the

people as well—it is this; that not only have they not read the sources—the texts of the religion—in addition to that, they have heard it and they consider it correct, not even retracing back to the texts, to check if

it is true or not. The dogmatic beliefs of people and their inability to vision the unity of another and for them to be considered unique (in the sense being different among the general populace,) is indigestible. In my recognition,

they can not encapsulate their brains around the notion that someone can benefit from life in a manner they hold to be true without ever looking, or having the will, to look into the matter and consequently decipher the matter

in their own fronts—as a result, deducing the matter with the comprehension. But, nay, nay, nay! “It is said, and so, I surrender.” “But, do you know it is there, and then, is it truly in your ability to prove

it? And have you?” “WHY DO YOU CARE? YOU DESERVE TO DIE BECAUSE YOU QUESTIONED MY BELIEFS!” To them, the religious people, religion is the head and the tail of their life. Without it, everything is in vain. And everything

else is unnecessary, if one divorces the reputation of religion in their life. Such stupidity lives in the heart of where I am birthed—where millions have been born without ever acquiring the chance to have a say in what they

might choose to be. To me, and all those who have the capacity to inquire, the courage to speak, while their tongues may be cut—we, the people of why—we are the ones who demand the dogmas to answer. To me,
the hearer of inquiry and the claimant of truth, this seems like the caging of a bird, meant to fly. The bird, only seeing what the cage looks like, not having a thin clue of what it is capable of.

The bird must soar—high, high, high… The case of interpretation of the senses of inquiry of these people is as a stuck brink in a wall—attached by cement, unbound, unwound—that is the penalty of taking your first, unasked breath in

a society of dogma. The incapacity of these people to bring something that could be tangled with the existence of knowledge and the empire of logic and intellect is a manifestation of their robust degeneracy and servility. The entrapping of

the human condition to explore is damaging, harming, and ultimately aching the house of human inquiry, from where it birthed the apostate of entangled chains and the knight in shining armor for the ascending force of the installment of human

reason. As far as I am aware, religion has served as the foundational basis for many societies across the globe. It has often acted as a motivating pillar—guiding populations, instilling meaning where there was little, and shaping the fabric of

collective life. In the unfolding program of human existence, religion has persisted—sometimes in full force with all its complexity and influence, and at other times in subtler, diminished forms. Regardless of its presence, the misuse of religion—or more precisely, the

mis-categorization and misapplication of it—has, at times, left monumental imprints on the course of human history. For instance, the uncalled-for destruction for the mis-categorizing the implication of human interest. 2. The Philosophy of Religion There is a misapplication in the

life of a human, which causes us to be left in the abyss of answers, for which the ground basis is, “because it is said.” And for them to be objective in this regard is a painful experience. The impossibility

of impregnating those of the people of questions, but only giving the ones manipulated at times of the birth of it, and not even having the spirited will to cast the shadow of the questions by bringing new explanations into

light, by unifying the whole into a term of logic and of reason is impractical, and so they reside in their holes of nonentity and resemble those of their predecessors. In this, we can count with us on the table

so far wedged and placed—the philosophy of religion: in my eyes, and in so far of my experience, it is a “philosophy without a why.” What? —a philosophy without a why? Does that make sense? One may perceive this in

many senses, or in a case not. i. This is what one might call a philosophy without a why—where one is not permitted to ask or inquire into the complexities of existence, or even into its most basic dimensions, in

order to deepen the contingent process of thought. If I may be allowed to further my statement, the presence of this unavailability of inquiry is a result of constant suppression and constant annihilation of pure reason, which is a commodity

upon which the pillars of thought are placed. Where a why has been traced, where a why has been placed, it was crushed either by placing irrelevant prose, or by bringing such people, with intentions veiled, to the court of

blasphemy—and then? Then the death is the companion of such an individual. The providers of answers of such a diminishing house of humanity, all a while where we have grown, is a possible explanation to the loss of its ground.

The mystics do not agree though. If the inquiry raises and the answers are not satisfactory, the blame is on the one who did ask, to the courageous, to the hero of art, of intellect, of predecessors of why to

the house of us, the birds who fly, they are the heroes. Answers are formulated in such a way where the counting of all its aspects, count little to none for this world, only to the part where it says,

because such-and-such has been recorded, hence, take it as is, and do not claim for it to be any less the than truth. ii. The second reason why some would call it a philosophy without a why is because the

people who uphold it—those who claim to defend it “righteously” amidst the ambiguity of life and the turmoil of existence—do not defend it by offering insight, but by closing the door to any. They assert answers in the face of

uncertainty not to illuminate, but to quell the anxiety of not knowing. In doing so, they mistake obedience for depth, repetition for understanding, and certainty for truth. They declare: “This is how it is, for it has been told so”—and

in that telling, no further question is permitted. To question is to betray, to doubt is to sin, and to seek an alternative is to exile oneself from their constructed whole. Thus, the “philosophy” becomes no philosophy at all—it becomes

an armor against the unknown, rather than a torch toward it. And this is why it is a philosophy without a why—not only because questions are forbidden, but because the questioner is already condemned. The absurdity of it is this,
in my sight; “it has been said, do not question or you will be lost.” Why will I be lost? I will leave that to those who may ponder on it. 3. The History of it In my observation, man

has always longed to know—not merely about things, but about the thingness of things—the hidden reality behind what is shown, the ineffable something which thought circles but never quite holds. This longing is not accidental; it is man’s essential hunger.

And with this, man surrendered himself to the known, and from the unknown he carved, not out of mastery, but out of the sheer capacity of wonder—a form. He captured the unknowable by means of the knowable, giving shape not

to answer it, but to bear the weight of asking. He connected the dots, the gaps, the potholes that begged to be filled—not out of certainty, but desperation. So, he added an able form, an objective thing, to solve the

thingness of it. Yet to question the dogma for its own-self is, in itself, a suicidal and manipulating manner of causing oneself to be an enemy of the commoner on the street. For these people of the street—those who once

feared and wondered—now claim to have seen. They, too, began to question the thingness, and in response, postulated their answers as truths, as if their statements aligned perfectly with what is. The testimony of such people, who sit with one

another and regard each other as allies, becomes the clasping of blind hands in a dark room—none seeing, yet all agreeing—as if truth could be born from mere agreement, as if certainty could be built by echo alone. And when

one dares to break this circle, when one simply imagines it might not be so—no, no, no... how could someone have such a thought? Where they could not form the knowing, and where their human limitation refused to acknowledge its

own abyss, they postulated what could only be described as a dramatically absurd, objectively held “truth.” Or so they call it: the truth. Thus, was born the false casualty—the slow, unnoticed death of genuine doubt. But they never once framed

themselves as opposite to truth. Nay. Instead, they clothed themselves in the garments of objectivity, wearing its name like a badge carved into their foreheads. And first—yes, first—they devised all that they knew and associated a specific entity to it.

They gave it names. Every known, physical or metaphysical aspect of living—rain, birth, breath, thought—was attributed to a being, a commander of that domain. These entities became the originators, the voices behind every effect. They had shape. They had stories.

They were adored not only for what they did, but for how and why they did it. Men did not merely believe—they requested from them. They pleaded, they traded, they trembled. This was submitted to for centuries. But then came

the reform—not by reason, but by order. With the evolution of the human thought, there came the origination of it being one. Not many, but one. The zeal of us, humans, in the past, made a political move disguised as

spiritual reform. We sought to unify—and in unifying, we made others submit. We handed them a new commander. But this commander was no God of mystery; he was the leader of the purge—the one with the will to allocate, to
dismantle hierarchy and frame its ruins into a classless society, a mold of obedience. They handed us a rulebook, not only of what we do and do not do, but of what we ought to and ought not to think,

to say, to desire. This was the initial phase of it. And the success of this operation—the successful implementation of meaningfulness, not meaning—was in the reverberation of new meanings being installed into us, replacing the spirit with its simulation. They

installed the structure, but removed the soul. They gave us names and faces, but forbade the question. And in doing so, they divorced us, to the degree of void. And it was accomplished. 4. The Spirit of it The prose

we have reached so far is the prose of alteration of the management of history, which is the actual causing brief momentary change in the spirit of our heirs. What do I mean by this? Let me make my statement
a tad bit clearer with an example of what has passed; let us step into the years in which the great war was fought in. Suppose the man of wrath, Hitler, had won the war, would the world have enough

space to have annulled the extremity of the regime and have progressed towards where it is now? The answer, which I may conclude, is no. And the answer to that is because the rigidness, the uni-spectralism to approach the one

notion as the true notion, and the expression of oneness as a trueness of the human extraordinary-self—is the reason why this will live. Moreover, the substance of both of them as a whole is the same in calculation in mine;

do as you are told, and question what you are allowed to question without the power of using the mind to criticize the model in use. Such is the case with which we are dealing with today. In many countries

where religion is used as a tool, whether the people are religious in their spirit of it, or it is the other way round, it is still a forceful medium. As an example—the Jews. Those who claim to be the
chose ones who are the beloved people of God and who ought to be treated as a people who are to be loved, worked for, feared, and as a whole, let be the masters of the selves. Such is the

case with the people of many as those who submit to the extravaganza of the cult they submit to, i.e., the blindfold of, “I am the one, the objective one, the one who knows, and the one who understands all—for
I have been guided by the powerful, the one who knows, and I am the one who has been given the right to judge by the gracious pattern of the one law, with me and my brothers and sisters.” My,

my, well, if all start to justify themselves only by following the pattern of the one divine law, then the primary predicament we ought to seed out the solution for is—which of you among the one law is the “right”

law? And have we lost out cognition to extract out the “right” from “wrong?” Perhaps we have not, but are so blind that we might be considered to have, as we do not consequent towards the end of it being

led by the beacon of truth or the way to extract the truth as is—philosophy.’ The ruins of us will remain, because the wars of this rhetorically bond formation of uni-spectral law and the same notion as the right one

is liquefying us, “I am correct, and my law/book says so.” Sure… If that is the statement of those who are correct, what exactly will be the end of the whole of us? The fixated mind of tutored one-sidedness as

held true or coherent to the fixed life is held objective, is the misery of the human existence. 5. Politics of it A tale of Love I: In the esoteric, the masked, the unfathomed—where nothing is seen yet too much

is felt. A place where the all-knowing, the divergent, the paramount, where the behemoths fail, where none can think but too little, where thoughts and light escape not, where man is naked in his fog of shades—the only locus where

time stops, and man’s erection of elucidation suffers the untimely loss of his deemed responses. The unparalleled, the masked, the unfathomed: love. When was he not in pain? Never until he was forced to love. The pain stems from the

meaning assigned to this very thing. Man turns from welcoming joy in his life, to plotting his immature and unplanned mind into the tapestry of time, where his elucidation flops, and where his matureness gives way to childness. The child

born now has to be submissive. No matter where the submission shall reside or pursue his swevens later on, his completeness unfolds. The residence of the child haunts him, even when his body turns pale and old. This inauguration of

the child back into his life, into his living, into his survival—that is his language now. Man forgets his purpose as he falls into the pit of inescapable, ineluctable, ineludible, ineliminable truth, beneath which the ultimate sorrow of the chest

speaks. Where the battleground is set, man himself is the battleground, the battle, the attacker, and the defender—ah, a balance he shall lose at all costs. The joys of his appearance, the bonding of his time, where his appearance speaks

to himself, but too little, where he understands nothing. That is love. The irrational, unexplainable part of his life, where man dies in sorrow, or speaks of the winds of the morrow, where he has no answers, where he is

filled to his beam—with too much of himself, where he neither buys nor sells ideas. Man stems only when he is at war with his peace. When he suffocates in nightmares and dreams, becoming a paradox, hyperaware and unaware of

his surroundings. The effect of love is tremendous. It is designed, embedded into us, so that our dearest part—our self—is encompassed in the eyes of the second. Love is both disease and cure. It is man’s safe haven, his protection,

where he lives and breathes, where he is summed into the greatest summation, for his contemplation, where he is transformed into a child, into a molding entity, the dearest he can ever be. In the scaffolding effect of hyperawareness caused

by love, man calls himself a beast—yet a child beast. He is blocked from thought, barricaded from stringing his liberty. That is the seed of man, the formation of his new form. Like a child, he does not see the

effect—the drug that has induced in him the child: love. Ah, my dear readers, love encapsulates the core of us humans. It is a dangerous road. It teaches the art of living. It makes the dead alive, and the alive,
dead. It does not pass. II. Is it a state or a lifelong process? Some call it a state of being. A state of living in a patch of life, as many deem it. The state of thinking must be

forgotten, and a state of pure irrational leaned toward: a place—the pure beginning of the demise of query, where the soul is given its existence. Is love for the weak? —what, for the weak? Nay, what hypocrisy is that? What

dissolution of vastness of time is that? How does man give himself, not even knowing he is, in the most chaotic way, without fighting, but battling at the same time. The confusion, my dear readers, those who have come with
me so far, is beyond contemplation. It is beyond understanding. It is beyond the common man; it is more than the one who does not seed his own self into the body of another. It is more than us, it

is more than oneness, than unity of the-self. It is the completeness of duality. But the completeness has its cost, the cost arises by indebting thyself with the sorrowful, painful, and unbearable, wedded with the strings of ultimate gaiety. There

exists nothing beyond love which requires an untiring battle, nothing is more demanding than love. Nothing is more requiring of the-self than love. To be invested in love is the greatest thing a human may be granted to achieve. To

be invested in something, with peak devotedness, warmth, and aroha for something or someone. The investment of a human’s communion from the guts of themselves is the dearest gift they can give you. But what has man gotten in return?

What have I gotten in return? Why do I want something in return when I am giving myself anyway? Should man be utterly selfless and nothing more? Shall he form his head around the masks of others’ truth? What shall
man do when he is in love? Ayesha, that was her name. From her, I can derive the grander and larger meaning of love. Adeena was one of the key pillars of my formative theory of love. For her unity
has ordered me to form my ability to love. Her lessons of love were the ones from which I had learned the true nature of what it is to love. The price of love, the power of it, the seeding

her is the irrational approach of love, the irrational tradition of love. The Religious Man is the Nihilist: Why do I say that? Why do I speak of such a thing? Are they not full of meaning—God? God is their

meaning, their clinging and uprooting, stemming, and erecting of the-self being. Why do I say such things? Is not God their helpful companion? —what? Is he or is he not? What is it that I see: he… he is not?!
What a misery for the religious man. But how…? Ah, God was never there. And even if he was, he never gave the religious man the power to help himself, he let him suffer in his own name. That is
the God you worship, oh religious man? But what of it, what does it matter to him? What does it matter to the one who doth not imagine outside of the realm of his obedience to the imaginary God? Does

God even exist? Let us inquire the stray dog. Freedom: The crow was not capable of drinking the water, until he broke the rules and added the pebbles. Not a moral stance my dear reader. Meaning: Man has always wandered

aimlessly in the wanderings of life. But his aimlessness is accompanied by his strangeness of interpretation which sighs with him and his conformity towards the creation he will impregnate of the entirety of the populus of migration, towards the newly

formed togetherness—but halt! One in them will create something anew: the traitor, the philosopher. Meaning is subjective and holds weight only when it arrives to the conclusive representation of the person. What even is meaning? Fixations: Nothing is wrong, nothing

is either right. Wrong, in addition to right, is just a fabrication of man’s mind: it is a reason given by man to the meaningless development of his own. How do you judge the right way? By the way the

creator has formulated his jottings. The givers of meaning fabricate to be the prior holders of the imaginative body of the whole, whereas the rest are not even imagined to be the factual—the givers of meaning are as lost as

the others. Perhaps, they play not to be, but in the reality of it, ah, they are, they are. Right and wrong are creations of a mere mind, which capitalizes the coercive force it possess to charge the eliminating capabilities
of those who guard against them. To music: Melody to my ears, to the one who dances, to the one who feels and is free to the one who thinks of his creation. The one who is the mover—the one

who is the dancer. The one who portrays everything in a moving, fixing way. Music is the envelopment, and digestive by the alive. To music humans pay a summation so extravagant that its measurement is unfathomable. The true offices of

human cognition and human adoration is the development towards the totality of liking of music. The dancers are wedded to music. The Dancers: Who is the dancer? —the one who lives. Of Friends: The wanderer, the one who does not

understand the world around him, the one who does not form the truths around him, by stamping them down with his hand—he, walks alone. The wanderer has friends along the path. The true companion is himself, that is the only

true companion he has. The rest come and walk. But the wanderer has known that, he has accepted that, and has the acceptance, that perhaps the case might be so. He who has the attainability of absolute friendship has been

desired—the special wanderer. The prior type is not any lesser either. Confusions: Always confusion, always. Never have I been patterned to not be confused, to not be entitled to my one string of thought. I am flued; I am open

to the thoughts and understandings of others. I know certain things. However, confusion is the emanating pillar of my thought. For if I was not confused, I shan’t have had a very precise and modeled perspective. But what is my
perspective: ask the stray dog. My, my, for also he shan’t know, as far as it is, I am unaware of it either. The Ugly man: To the one who resides in the seat of the pedestrians, the one who

does not see beyond the other side. Is he blind? –perhaps, he is, perhaps he does not see. Perhaps? Does he or does he not? Ah, the forceful nature—yes, he is. But not the blind you imagine—nay—the one you shall

not fathom. The ugly man sees only that which he deems to be true, he is a believer. The one who thinks of a singular idea, to be the summation of the unifying glory of the subordinating, confusing, to the

self—the untimely believer. Then there are the knower and the doubter. The knower knows the laws, he sees the laws, that it is. Then arrives the strangest one: the doubter. He does not know. He does not understand, he tries.
He what? Why does he try? Because there resides a fire in him, which is too much to put out. He is not the one who sees beyond himself, but sees beyond the comprehension of all else. What else? The

world. He sees himself. The self is beyond understanding, it is the most daunting task to find the miseries and the difficulties assigned with the self. To understand or understand not, the self remains, and the doubter is of the

former category. The doubter: the pained, the lied to, the liar himself, the one whom doth not wish to be understood by all, but by one or a few—the excellent would be for him to be understood by himself—the second

best: by the one he loves. The doubter is always confused. He is in the woods of eternity,: “The woods are lovely, dark and deep, But I have promises to keep, And miles to go before I sleep, And miles

to go before I sleep.” He has miles to go, my dear readers. Do you? The ugly man does not understand the actuality of the world; he has his delusions succumbed him to the factual understanding of the universe. But

is it understanding? Can a man frame it as such? Will he be able to frame it as such? Nay, he doth not understand—his capabilities tremble, they fall, and he fails to understand. The framer of objectivity, the one who

draws all else to be false and terms the world with his subjective sense to path way for his objectivity, and his demeanor towards the thwarting world, he thinks of himself a God. The Prophet: The prophet believes he is

God. He preaches God likely the way he sees himself. The prophet sees God just the way he sees himself. The worshipers of a religion are worshiping his ideas—the prophets’ ideas. As God is a tale of old and imagination,

the prophet molds all around the God and signifies everything to be the case of God. But the fact is, he believes in no God, he believes in himself. In the scales of depth of thought, he, the prophet, the

enemy of living, the divine myth, the forger of falsifying testimonies—him. He is not a philosopher; he is the dogmatist. The weight of the own-self: It is not the emptiness we fear; it is the weight of the company of

the own-self. The gravitating self-contemplating, reliance on the summation of the centered scrutiny, combined with the prose of the imaginative body, for the amie of the intensity, springing from within, the undoubted doubt, where strings form within us. The untamed,

the un-petted, the beast that lies within. The awakening of the one form by the amor in addition with meaty combination, the self-loathing, the talker, exuberant one, with his mighty-fervor does he stretch himself. The majesty, centered to the core

of contemplation restores the doubter to his undefined degree. Truth is what he seeks, reality is what he decodes—nay, not the unrealistic, the metaphysical, nay, nay, nay… the one in front of him, which he demands, sees, or perhaps aims

to see. The lonelier the man, the more he sees himself. The greater the star, the brighter it is, the more it pulls under the impression of its gravity—it is the highest star. The doubter is the star. The self,

the difficult query, which is almost undoable to task it out. No objectivity: How is it possible that not always is a turnout event perpetuated as a continuation of a responding event — which has occurred in the fabric of

time — nor is it a culminating event, nor an appreciating sense of duality, nor a despondence to the forthcoming. All else trembles, all else halts. Nothing of man resides; nothing of him is in congregation with the spirited and

the high-landing. What it is, rather, is the turning out of events being shuffled — not lawlessly, but through that probability which pretends at law, that unseen arithmetic of the random. Is it the case that a man must, or
that he ought to be loved, or must be the beloved of another, even though they are merely liked by one another — or by their presence? Let us inquire, instead, the stray dog — for he too moves by

those rules that may or may not repeat, whose steps seem without design yet follow the deep rhythm of uncertainty. The randomness which has encapsulated the happenings of man’s life — which governs it without his realization — that is

precisely what he has been avoiding. The randomness has rules, but those rules may or may not repeat; they are probability masquerading as disorder. The repetition of an event is nearly impossible, perhaps truly impossible. The conclusive point of them

is never known. Nor is it possible that these rules will direct the appreciation of such happenings — nay, it shall not; it does not always occur. The objectivist has no say when it comes to the world. If something
happens — which it does — he deems it a miracle. Why, you disgusting pig, are you unable to see and visualize the occurrence of the random trajectory? Do you have a sense? Or do you lack one? Ah, I
see not what your dismemberment is — not yet, at least. What must the objectivist claim as all else to be false? Perhaps he may, for he is the knower of truth — in his head. But is truth not

unknown? Is not my path mine, and your path yours? What a lie — for even our paths, too, are governed by the probabilities we deny, the randomness we name as fate, the pattern that never repeats but forever governs.

Lost for words: The lonelier the man, the silently he weeps, the less the listeners hear, the more the deaf know. The more he weeps, the stronger he gets, the more he can handle—weep more. The lonelier I am, the
worst I feel, the deeper I mean, the more I conceive, the more I become lonely and hence, the more I become more. Loneliness is a drug none can fathom. None can imagine, and for all I care, none can

print on their hearts. The forgotten words: Now, that I have been penning down my words for quite some time, I must confess for my surety exists not. There are days in which I breathe proper, and qualifying thoughts, but

my, my, do I not pen them down. Confinement: Confined by what? The strings of him, or the weight of myself? I call it freedom, yet every choice is a command obeyed. Man must serve—himself or another. Even rebellion is
a form of worship. We submit, even in denial. But is a slave not a blind follower? Yes, he is. And if the slave-man, as mentioned above, is a rebel to the notions passed, is he is still a slave?
In this case scenario, he is not. But what more scenarios do you need? Can a man be a slave even as a king? But can a king not be a slave? Ah, the politicians of my country: Sharif family,

and the outrageous and self-awarded field marshal, the submitter, the jahil, the human amongst beasts. Regardless, what is the crux of it? Slavery to oneself is freedom? But what else is freedom? However, is it not that we are influenced

by others? But does that make us slaves? Do we not wrestle with ideas and then see them fit to assign them to ourselves? Ah, but the slave does not outgrow the ideas they have battled with, they objectify them

and signal them to be the bridge of their life, for they walk this bridge and then die as they have crossed it. The rest—they swim—no bridges for them. Rule Book: “The book of life”. That is the way to
live the life which is yours. But what in fact is yours if it is assigned to the rule book itself? How come it is possible that a single word or text of an author is the summation of the

life you are pursuing to live? Are you pursuing to live this life? The life you live, my dear reader: is it worthy of the culmination to live once more? —Perhaps many a-times more? The causing agent of the whole

caused is the seizing and agenting further annihilation of the masses to produce the maximum taste of the so-called innate life, controlling and restricting each step of living, leaving no space for deviation or escape. Now, perhaps the “innate life”

is what one requires, but from where doe this innate life stem from? From where does it grow its seeds: You, perhaps? If it is so, then by definition the whole case is resting upon your explanation and you yourself

are the body of dictating lies. And what is more is that you are claiming the objective sense of the self if anything. This further results in the antithesis of the previous culminated peak: you are merely falling and failing.

Consequentially, resting the case of your rule book to be the utter biased version of your saying and doing. But where do we dictate that this rule book ever is the saying of an author, that is, a man? Perhaps

by gazing long enough into the scene of the question only to discover that the so-called saying of the dreamer of the falsifying realm of metaphysics is only damning itself and is only releasing its fumes onto us by deploying

the imaginative body of the man; which man? The metaphysician. The one who uses the tool without testing anything at all. But having that said, are all metaphysicians as such? Nay. However, I will not have it lightly on the

many. Those of them who deem the testable world inferior to their untestable or intangible realm, in addition, those who break the chains and view the world with the scope of the imaginative realm, those of them who formulate the

arguments based on the things alien to the living, and without setting step into the natural—those are the pure targeted ones. Now, the normative line of resurrection birthed by the all-true followers of the rule book are generalizing the claims

of that rule book. Sometimes, even the question of the authenticity of the rule book seems to be disadvantageous. A rule book for the praise of everything is just to bring oneself to the utmost variety of maximum, to further

the statement of the said or noted without having to engage with the do-ability of the thing or the task at hand. It attempts to praise all of creation, but in reality it is not. It is hypnotizing, almost casting

a spell on the reader, which brings the “oneself” to the peak of living, almost like a shot of marijuana. And this peak has a variety of disinfectants, conflicts, contradictions, praises, worthiness, all around, it is the maximum of it
all. They parade themselves as lovers of truth, even the bitter kind, so long as it marches in step with their rule book. But the moment truth pulls in another direction — as it has, and as it does —

they abandon the pursuit and retreat back into the book’s shade. They clutch its words as if the mere act of holding them makes them victorious. And so the truth they claim to serve becomes secondary to the text they
worship. Have you ever wondered why it is the case that not inquiring of tasking a task with the fervor you are engaging yourself with, ever seem to weigh you down? The rule book is by any man… it is

by something, or someone else: a God. Ye, the true and mighty God. Impossible of delivering a falsifying reality. Furthermore, any contradiction—contradiction? Nay, nay! The answer is: “Any word in this book is correct. That which we do not understand

is the product of our misunderstanding and nothing more. Secondly, all else is veiled and masked under the complexity of the reigning sense of The Al-Mighty.” And that, my careful reader, is the peak of their argument. Perhaps, the true

lining is hidden, and perhaps the web is masked. But who has masked it, is the proper inquiry. Who? God. God? Who is that? Prove him, and there he is. “He is beyond contemplation. Every race, every community, every person

that tried to overcome the intensity of the Al-Mighty were overcome by him. And are not the signs in the rule books enough? Are not the signs of the rule books proved? And all of them and accurate. And those

which are “out of place”, they must be viewed with the lens of metaphors, or as mentioned previously: they are not to be contemplated by a commoner, or a human, or anyone for that sense. Even the takes which seem

out of place, those are merely for our protection and hence, we do not know all, and the Al-Mighty does.” Bravo, bravo! That is the pure form of rhetoric there, dear readers. Do you not sense the hypocrisy in the

sayings of these individuals and how intensely they fall into the pit of rhetoric only for them to evacuate their senses into the underlining form of sayings of their God, gods, or even Prophets? On Music: One dances and moves

with it. You have your own musical tastes to give your life a certain expression that enlightens you. How can it be “forbidden”? According to certain religions, music is the enemy of man. Let us think this through. How can

they speak of such a human activity as forbidden and unwanted? How is it possible that music becomes the enemy of religions? Music is not neutral. It shapes emotion. A melody can awaken nostalgia; a rhythm can energize the body;

lyrics can direct admiration, resentment, longing, or defiance. At a wedding, a specific kind of music is expected because it produces a particular emotional atmosphere. Different contexts demand different sounds because different sounds organize different responses. Music, therefore, is a

carrier of ideas that amplifies feeling. A song or melody may evoke emotions of rebellion if it contains hatred or speaks against a topic. The same goes for recitations. A recitation does invoke certain feelings. Music is a carrier of

ideas that amplifies emotion. When those ideas oppose dominant norms, music becomes a vehicle of rebellion. When they support dominant norms, music becomes a tool of reinforcement. Religious texts and their recitations can amplify a sense of hatred when read

in a certain way. This aligns with the idea that melodies can be used to generate feelings of rebellion toward something or someone. Thus, religious people may harbor a sense of hatred toward those who are mentioned in their texts

as opposing their teachings. Returning to our original account: why do religions instill revulsion toward music in the minds of their followers? If the answer is not yet clear, I will make it clear. It is for the same reason

that they do not allow one to listen to the recitation of another text. Music is sung from the chest of another, and if it targets a notion and its followers accept it, then that notion (religion, in this context)

receives the spotlight. However, this is not the spotlight it wants to be in. If emotion shapes allegiance, then any institution concerned with preserving allegiance must be attentive to competing emotional influences. A song that redirects admiration or loyalty toward

an alternative vision of life competes. It offers another center of meaning. For a system that claims ultimate authority, such competition is not trivial. Music creates a framework that can contribute to the weakening of religion itself. Music organizes emotion.

Emotion organizes allegiance. Any system that seeks to monopolize allegiance will regulate competing emotional forces. Therefore, restrictions on music may function as a method of preserving doctrinal control. On the concept of the Unseen: There exists a peculiar habit within

man: he speaks of what he has never encountered as though it stood before him in daylight. He has not seen it, not sensed it, not verified it. Yet because another claims to have seen it, he inherits the vision.

Testimony becomes sight. Repetition becomes certainty. And certainty, once repeated enough, hardens into truth. Consider the claim of unseen beings such as the Djinn—said to be created of fire, said to have lived before man, said to exist alongside us

yet beyond our perception. The authority for their existence is scripture. The defense of their invisibility is that they are meant to be unseen. The proof of their reality is that someone trustworthy affirms it. When pressed further, the answer

stabilizes into a final refuge: God said so. Observe the structure carefully. The being cannot be sensed. It cannot be measured. It cannot be verified. Its absence from observation is not a difficulty for the claim but its reinforcement. If

you cannot see it, that is because you are not meant to. If you cannot test it, that is because it transcends testing. Thus the claim protects itself from every possible challenge. It becomes untouchable not by strength, but by

design. Here the philosopher must pause. What qualifies something as true? If a claim lies beyond perception and beyond verification, on what ground does it stand? If the only support is authority, then belief rests not on evidence but on

submission. This may be psychologically powerful, but it is not epistemically sufficient. To accept what cannot in principle be examined is to lower the threshold of belief indefinitely. Once that threshold collapses, nothing prevents the admission of any invisible entity.

The sky may host unicorns. The air may conceal kingdoms. A claim becomes immune not because it is true, but because it is insulated. The unseen, then, is not the issue. The issue is the standard by which we admit

something into reality. If the standard is testimony alone, belief multiplies without limit. And if testimony is not verifiable for such a massive claim, how must we call it the end? If the standard is verification, many cherished ideas fall

silent. Between these two thresholds stands the human mind, deciding what it will allow to exist. However, they do not listen, they do not pay heed. Those pigs of the subordinating notions, all in all, they are scums. What lies

behind the veil, succumbs the entirety of the audience as their fiction creates the bubble of masterful illusion for them to polish their highs and extend their pathetic lives as adjusted, and falsely breathe meaning into their lives. But here,

we must also resist this unwanted and stupefying ideas. And in that decision, more than in any unseen being, lies the true power. The unseen: That which cannot be touched by inquiry is not strong — it is merely sheltered.

Systems: Man’s disturbance begins when his mind tries to impose itself upon the world of action. We live within systems, and yet we constantly interfere with them. The world operates through systems, and without them human society would not function.

Order, coordination, and long-term progress depend on structure. In the modern age this need has only intensified. Institutions, rules, and organized processes allow millions of people to act together toward shared goals. Yet systems also create their own limitations. What

allows order can also suppress change. When rules become rigid, they restrict thought and discourage deviation. Many breakthroughs occur only when someone steps outside the established structure. In that sense, systems both support and resist progress. They provide direction and

stability, but they can also slow the very innovation that pushes humanity forward. Human life therefore moves in a tension between order and disruption. We rely on systems to live, but progress often begins when someone questions them. These systems

unlock a certain rule for life, and by that rule, millions and billions of people abide. And this allows for peace and prosperity. However, is it worth it to live in peace that comes from falsity? When another clash appears,

as is does in the modern world; different ideas clash--what then, is the outcome? Is it not war? A war that annihilates all that comes forth in its way? However, any idea that is proposed, and turns out to be
in opposition causes annihilation in one way or another. These structures, when followed by people dictate societies
